lesson.title: AI all around you
lesson.subtitle: Where you meet AI, and what it really is

video.title: AI all around you
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — teacher at the same school (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A secondary-school science lab in the morning: benches, a wall chart of the water cycle, students in local uniform. Mr Okafor stands at the front with one hand up; only three students raise theirs. He smiles, as if he knows something they don’t.
scenes.animation: Three hands pop up one after another (150 ms each). Quick push-in on Mr Okafor’s grin.
scenes.narration: Hands up if you’ve used AI today. Only three of you? I’d say every one of you has, and before you even got to school!

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and the AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: what AI is, where you meet it, and what it isn’t.

scenes.visual: A phone alarm screen showing 06:00, then a calculator showing the same sum twice with the same answer. A small rule card beside each: written by a person.
scenes.animation: The alarm rings (a gentle shake); the calculator answer appears twice, identically.
scenes.narration: Some machines only follow rules that a person wrote. Your alarm rings at six because you set it for six. A calculator gives the same answer to the same sum, every time. Useful, but they never learn anything new.

scenes.visual: A teenager on a bus watches a football clip on a phone, then another. A third clip slides up as a suggestion. Behind the phone, faint rows of thousands of tiny viewers watching clips.
scenes.animation: The suggestion card slides up (300 ms); the crowd of tiny viewers fades in behind.
scenes.narration: Other machines learn from examples. Watch two football clips, and your video app lines up a third. Nobody wrote that rule just for you. The app learned from what millions of people watched next, and it made a guess about you.

scenes.visual: Clean card with the AI chip. Three boxes joined by arrows: a stack of examples, a pattern (puzzle piece), a best guess (target).
scenes.animation: Boxes appear one by one, arrows drawing between them.
scenes.narration: So here’s what most people mean by AI today. It’s a computer system that learns patterns from lots of examples. Then it uses those patterns to make predictions: best guesses about things it doesn’t know yet.

scenes.visual: A dusty school pitch. A goalkeeper in gloves faces a penalty. Thought-bubble tally: twenty past penalties by this striker, most arrows pointing left. She dives left; the ball goes right this time.
scenes.animation: Tally arrows fill in quickly; the dive is a simple slide; the ball rolls the other way.
scenes.on_screen_text: Like a goalkeeper at a penalty
scenes.narration: Think of a goalkeeper facing a penalty. She’s watched this striker take twenty penalties, and most went to the left. So she dives left. That’s a prediction from patterns. It isn’t mind reading, and sometimes she’s wrong.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor beside two pictures: a street light switching on at dusk, and a phone map with a red, slow bus route. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Mr Okafor slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A street light switches on at six every evening. A map app warns that your bus route is slow today. Which one is AI?

scenes.visual: The ‘map app’ card gets a check badge. Split screen: the street light with a simple timer dial; the map with many faint trip lines feeding one red ‘slow’ segment.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); trip lines draw across the map.
scenes.narration: The map app. It learned from the trips of millions of phones how traffic usually moves, and it predicts today’s delays. The street light just follows a timer that someone set.

scenes.visual: A student’s morning, four quick panels: unlocking a phone with a glance, typing in the class WhatsApp group with word suggestions, a voice note turning into text, a spam folder quietly catching a scam.
scenes.animation: Panels flip in one by one, about two seconds each.
scenes.narration: Now think about your morning again. Face unlock learned from many faces how to tell yours apart. Your keyboard guesses your next word. Voice notes can be turned into text. And a spam filter hides scam messages before you see them.

scenes.visual: A phone chat: the chatbot’s reply ‘I understand’. Under it, the reply splits into word tiles, each with a small likelihood bar. A heart icon with a line through it.
scenes.animation: Word tiles separate; bars fill (1 s).
scenes.on_screen_text: Predicts, but doesn’t think or feel
scenes.narration: But AI doesn’t think or feel the way you do. When a chatbot writes “I understand”, it’s predicting words that usually fit. It has no feelings, and it doesn’t know what’s true in your life.

scenes.visual: The Darsi ‘Guess the next word’ lab on a phone: the sentence ‘In the morning the pupils open their ___’, four bars (books, notebooks, windows, phones) and a temperature slider from ‘Predictable’ to ‘Creative’.
scenes.animation: Bars grow; the slider moves right and the bars even out; a word drops into the gap.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: guess the next word
scenes.narration: After this video, open the lab. You’ll see the start of a sentence: “In the morning the pupils open their”. Bars show how likely each next word is: books, notebooks, windows or phones. Move the temperature slider, and watch the choices get safer or more surprising.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina holds up a phone with a chatbot message: ‘I’m so happy to help you!’ Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A chatbot writes, “I’m so happy to help you!” Does it really feel happy?

scenes.visual: The ‘No’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines and the takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Points arrive one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: No: it predicts words that fit, but it feels nothing. Remember: some machines only follow rules, while AI learns patterns from examples. What AI gives you is a prediction, a best guess. And best guesses can be wrong.

scenes.visual: A student’s exercise book open at a page titled ‘AI diary’, with a few entries: keyboard, map, video app, each with ‘it predicted…’. Mr Okafor smiles beside it. End card: Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Diary lines write themselves in; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: keep an AI diary for one day. Every time you meet AI, on your keyboard, a map or a video app, write down what it predicted. Then ask yourself: was it right?

checkpoints.prompt: A street light switches on at six every evening. A map app warns that your bus route is slow today. Which one is AI?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the map app learned from many trips how traffic usually moves, and it predicts today’s delays.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the street light only follows a timer someone set. The map app learned patterns from many trips and predicts delays.

checkpoints.prompt: A chatbot writes “I’m so happy to help you!” Does it really feel happy?

options.text: No — it predicts words that fit

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it predicts words that usually fit. It has no feelings.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — saying it isn’t feeling it. A chatbot predicts words that usually fit; it has no feelings.
